lesson.menu_desc: Give an opinion on somebody else's work -- present perfect vs past simple
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 3 -- Saying What You Think
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Pedro Henrique Tadeu Alves da Silva | Lesson 3 -- Saying What You Think

listenings.text: Before anybody plays anything today, one rule, and it is the only rule I enforce. When it is your turn to respond, you say what you heard before you say what you think. Not good, not bad. What you heard. The drums came in late. The second verse was shorter than the first. I lost the words at the end of the chorus. That is it. And the reason is not politeness, it is accuracy. Ninety percent of what people call feedback is a guess about the intention, and half the time the guess is wrong. If you tell me the drums came in late, I know something true about my own song that I could not hear any more, because I have listened to it four hundred times. If you tell me you did not like it, I have learned nothing, and neither have you. The opinion is welcome, but it goes second, and it goes in one sentence.

The worst note I have ever been given was three words long: make it pop. I asked what pop meant and the person could not say, so I spent eleven days guessing, and in the end I delivered the first version with the vocal two decibels louder and they said yes, perfect, that is it. Eleven days. The best note I have ever been given was also short, and it came from a drummer who does not produce anything. She said, I stopped listening at one minute forty. She did not say why, she did not say fix it, she just said where. And she was right, because that is exactly where the second chorus repeats without changing anything. I cut eight bars and the problem disappeared. Since then, when I listen to somebody else's work, I write down the timecode where my attention left the room. It is the only note I have ever given that people thank me for a year later.

extra_audio.text: Pedro says he has listened to the track three times, and that the chorus is the part he remembers. He says the hook lands, and that the second verse is where it stops working for him. He thinks the strings are a bit overdone, and he calls it a nitpick and not a problem. He points out one subtle thing: the drums come in half a bar late, and it works. He suggests tightening the bridge by four bars, so that the whole thing holds up. Then he asks the other person what they thought of his own track.
